newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Bank bosses under spotlight in Vietnam fraud trial.
newsitem.headline: Bank bosses under spotlight in Vietnam fraud trial.

text.p: Former top executives of Vietnam's leading commercial bank and a deputy governor of the central bank were cross-examined in Ho Chi Minh City People's Court on Monday as the Tamexco fraud trial entered its fourth day.
Four former executives of two banks are among 20 people who are accused of siphoning off some $40 million of state money through Tamexco, a company linked to the ruling Communist Party.
The central State Bank of Vietnam's deputy governor, Chu Van Nguyen, was summoned to give evidence at the trial but has not been named as a defendant.
The Saigon Times Daily said one of the four bankers, former Firstvina Bank Deputy Director Tran Linh, had already been questioned in court on Saturday about loans granted to Tamexco.

"Tran Linh said he signed contracts to lend a total of $7.75 million to Tamexco without abiding by banking regulations, but he noted that State Bank of Vietnam officials gave the green light to the implementation of these loan contracts," it said.

The other bankers in the dock include two former director-generals of state-owned Vietcombank, Nguyen Manh Thuy and Nguyen Van De, both of whom had previously chaired the board of Firstvina Bank, a Vietcombank affiliate.
The trial, which is likely to continue for at least four more days, is expected to end with a death sentence for the key defendants if they are found guilty.
The key figure in the case is Pham Huy Phuoc, director of the now-defunct import-export company.
He alone is accused of misappropriating some $27 million, allegedly channelling huge sums of cash to friends and relatives and even gambling away five cars in a card game.
Foreign journalists have not been granted permission to attend the trial.
However, the domestic press has been encouraged to give wide coverage of the case to demonstrate the government's offensive against corruption.

The army newspaper, Quan Doi Nhan Dan, said on Monday that while the whole country was on guard against "hostile forces" from outside, an "internal enemy" -- corruption -- had risen up to threaten the revolutionary cause.
